This is an audit, not the Results structure

Nine questions is the right granularity for deciding what to build and what to trust. It is the wrong granularity for a dissertation, which would read as a lab notebook — question, answer, question, answer. The sections below collapse into six Results chapters, and the collapse is where the argument lives.

  1. R1 · the phenotype§1 + §3 — two qualitatively different forms of forgetting. Changing the scenario changes the geometry; changing the rule does not.
  2. R2 · the setup§2 — a stable operating regime where the dynamics converge to the same fixed point, so later differences are not settling artefacts. Keep it short; it is a precondition, not a chapter.
  3. R3 · the comparison§4 + §5 — PC ahead in Class-IL, behind in Domain-IL, and the sign difference amplifies with depth. Then: does prospective configuration itself account for it?
  4. R4 · why two scenarios§6 — repeated alternation. Class-IL ping-pongs between incompatible solutions; Domain-IL contracts toward a joint one.
  5. R5 · localisation§7 + §8 — output competition on one side, representation-dependent failure on the other, both stated as evidence rather than conclusion.
  6. R6 · does fixing it help§9 — the intervention ranking, and the scale that makes PC's one to three points readable.
1

What does forgetting look like?

Needs rebuildingOne figure, rebuilt. What exists today understates its own point.

Why these figures answer the question

This figure defines rather than compares, and a single fixed-budget seed does that better than a ten-seed mean: nothing is smoothed, the whole trajectory is visible, and the per-class lines carry a mechanism the reader needs later. Everything downstream refers to three things named here — the switch, the plateau, and the crossing.

2

The setup, and why each choice was made

Partly answeredOrdered generic → forgetting-specific. The metric is the climax of the section, not a footnote in it.

Why these figures answer the question

Ordered from choices any network needs to the choices this question needs: architecture, then specification, then PC's own control, then statistics, then the metric. The metric column is last because it is the most forgetting-specific decision in the report and the one everything downstream rests on — it is the section's conclusion, not a footnote. Critically, every justification here is single-rule. Choosing crossover because it preserves the PC-versus-backprop sign would select the instrument by the answer it gives on the comparison it will then be used for — the error CLAUDE.md already forbids for learning rates. Here the endpoint fails as the stopping point moves, crossover fails as the learning rate rises, and the competence-matched rule falls out of the two failures. The rule comparison is not mentioned until §3.

3

Does each rule forget, and does it look the same in each scenario?

AnsweredThe four panels exist. They have never been assembled into the one grid that makes the point.

Why these figures answer the question

Read as a 2×2 these four panels make a point no single panel makes: changing the scenario changes the shape of forgetting; changing the rule does not. Down a column the trajectories are near-superimposable; across a row they are different families — one collapsing onto an axis, one stopping on a shelf. That asymmetry is what §6 has to justify formally, and it is why §4's comparison must be reported per scenario.

4

Which rule is better, and is that stable?

Partly answeredAnswered on three axes. The consolidation that makes it one claim has never been drawn.

Why these figures answer the question

The answer is small, real, and sign-flipped by scenario. A one-to-three-point effect at a single architecture invites the dismissal that it is a quirk of H=32, depth 1 — and the sweeps refute that in an unexpected way. The effect is not fragile, it is systematic, growing with depth in both directions at once. The replay panel keeps it honest: the problem is solvable, and PC's uplift is about a seventh of what a memory mechanism buys, so this is a small real effect rather than a headline.

5

Is the difference actually caused by prospective configuration?

Not answeredThe mechanism at the centre of the thesis — and the one the source paper credits — is never measured against the outcome.

Why these figures answer the question

Everything up to here is behavioural. None of it touches what makes PC PC — that the hidden state relaxes to a configuration the feedforward pass would not produce, and the update is computed against that. This section closes the gap from two directions. Target alignment is the mechanism the source paper credits, so testing it is not optional; that it fails is a result about their claim, not a tidy-up. The displacement is our own measure of the same thing and is thrown away on every update as a convergence check. Relating it to ΔW and retention converts the spine from "task structure → forgetting → PC vs backprop" into "task structure → network dynamics → prospective configuration → weight change → forgetting" — the claim the title implies.

6

Why are these two investigations, not one?

Not answeredThe strongest section available, and almost none of it is built. Weight-space geometry is the part that makes it more than a pretty plot.

Why these figures answer the question

The split must be earned twice, and it is earned decisively on one axis and not at all on another. Structurally it is not arguable: Class-IL has five output units receiving no positive target during task 2, so suppression is physically available; Domain-IL's shared units make it impossible. Empirically the geometry argument is the strongest available — a loop and a spiral are different kinds of behaviour, not different amounts of one — and the weight-space panels are what stop it being a pretty picture. A scalar contraction measure turns "it looks like a loop" into "the network returns to a substantially different state after each switch, while Domain-IL's progressively contracts". The joint-pretraining panel then asks the sharper question the others set up: whether the difference is about finding a joint solution or holding one. The tie-out draws the two measurements that behave the same in both scenarios as parallel lines rather than hiding them.

7

Class-IL — evidence for an output-competition component

Not answeredFour results point one way, one points the other — and that contradiction narrows the candidates rather than muddying them.

Why these figures answer the question

Four things point at output competition: digit identity, the output specification, masking's success, and the argmax-versus-probe gap. One points away — freezing the output layer recovers nothing — and it is the confirmation that should have been easiest to get. The title says component, not problem, because the evidence supports the former. But the contradiction narrows the candidates. Masking acts only on the training error, leaving argmax competing over all ten units at evaluation, and recovers +17.5. Freezing all of W2 also spares the task-1 output weights and recovers nothing — but additionally blocks task 2 from learning through the readout, forcing it into W1. That single difference is testable by freezing only the task-1 columns, and it splits cleanly. The trained probe attacks the same ambiguity from the representation side and the per-layer path from the weight side. Until one lands, the localisation is suggested, not established.

8

Domain-IL — evidence for a representation-dependent failure

Not answeredDifferent story, not the same story with smaller numbers. And there is no positive answer to "where".

Why these figures answer the question

Class-IL has five output units receiving no positive target, so it is an output-competition problem. Domain-IL has none, so whatever happens is in the representation or the shared readout — a different investigation, not the same one with smaller effects. The depth asymmetry supports that directly: a trunk variable helps one scenario and hurts the other. What this section lacks is a positive answer to "where". The pairing correlation is a clear negative result — publishable as a correction, not an explanation; freezing rules out the output layer uninformatively; no drift measurement exists under the current protocol. Reporting that plainly beats importing §7's readout story by analogy, which the Domain-IL data does not support.

9

What actually helps?

Partly answeredSix interventions measured. The ranking they jointly support has never been drawn.

Why these figures answer the question

This is where the argument lands, and it lands as a ranking rather than a single result. The two interventions that work substantially — replay and masking — either store the old data or change the readout. The ones that barely work add a penalty to the existing rule. The one that actively harms is the one the predictive-coding literature most often proposes. Nothing that modifies credit assignment alone recovers much. Read against §4, where PC's uplift is about a seventh of replay's, that is the project's conclusion on one axis.

What the whole thing adds up to

Predictive coding does not provide a general solution to catastrophic forgetting. Its prospective-configuration dynamics produce a small, scenario-dependent change in continual-learning performance — ahead in Class-IL, behind in Domain-IL, amplifying with depth in both directions — but the dominant source of forgetting lies in the interaction between task structure, output competition and representation stability. Explicit memory mechanisms are substantially more effective than modifying the credit-assignment rule alone.

Six of the thirteen builds are P1, and five of those six are instrumentation of runs that already exist rather than new experiments.
Every number is carried from progress.md, re-derived from the saved .npz arrays rather than from earlier notes. Where a figure and a note disagreed, the arrays were treated as ground truth. Nothing here requires new training except §2's activation check and §6's Class-IL alternation arm.
